verdict:
The steer is correct and my first plan was wrong in a way I can now prove with numbers rather than concede politely.

What I got wrong. (1) I decomposed the entire game for a 1920x1080 still. Every one of the 16 `judgeOn` fields said some version of "compare at matched 720px height against a bar panel." Not one piece carried a number. That decomposition builds a beautiful screenshot generator, not a game. (2) I let one measurement seduce me. I measured 29.6 ms/frame for a heavy scene and concluded "we are not restricted to a toy renderer." What I had actually measured was the still-capture path. I never measured the live loop. I measured it just now, on the current foundation, with fallback content only (103 draw calls, 60k tris): `?quality=live` runs at p50 200-566 ms/frame — 2 to 5 fps. An empty scene with the overlay off is still 100 ms/frame. That is 6x to 34x over budget before a single real piece exists, and it is not a content problem, it is the loop: `preserveDrawingBuffer:true` forces a per-frame copy, and every frame round-trips through a half-float render target plus a fullscreen resolve quad. I benchmarked that round trip in isolation: +17 ms at 0.52 MP on this box. Those choices are correct for accumulation capture and catastrophic for a game loop. I built one execution path and called a branch of it "live." There are two paths and I conflated them. (3) `engine.js:372` reads `liveT += SIM_STEP * 2` — the live loop advances simulated time by a constant per rAF callback, with no wall clock and no accumulator. That is frame-rate-dependent simulation wearing determinism as a costume: if a frame takes 200 ms the world still advances 16.7 ms, so the game runs in slow motion under load and every timing window is wrong. For a game whose premise is "timing is critical," that is a foundational defect sitting inside a frozen file. (4) `input.js` is 13 lines of KEYMAP plus a gamepad poll. Zero touch. The component the user just named the most important in the game had no implementation and no owner among 16 pieces. (5) The overlay is a fixed 1920x1080 Canvas2D fully redrawn every frame with glows and shadow blurs; that is unaffordable inside a 1.8 ms UI budget. (6) No piece owned game flow, so there was nowhere to put "entering a play must not hitch." (7) Quality was a two-value enum. The steer requires a measured, continuous, self-adjusting ladder.

What I am keeping. The registry/contract/fallback architecture is genuinely good and is the thing that makes 18 agents build in parallel; it gets extended, not replaced. The still-capture path survives completely untouched — `shoot.mjs`, `compare.mjs`, the 11 hero scenes, byte-identical PNGs, the 720px matched-height A/B — but it is now explicitly declared a SECOND execution path against a SECOND bar with NO frame budget, and no perf claim may ever cite it. The rig split (anatomy | pose | uniform), ShotSpec, texlab, rng, the determinism linter and the progress board all stand. `typeface-lettering`'s round-1 build stands. Most visual briefs stand as content — what changes is that each now ships a rung ladder and a counted structural budget instead of an unbounded appetite.

What I am re-cutting. The spine is now: touch controller, tick-exact timing model, fixed-timestep sim, animation runtime, game flow, live HUD — priorities 1 through 6, built and judged before any fidelity piece. Every runtime piece is judged on a number a critic reads off a command. Visual pieces become dependent variables: each implements `applyRung(n)` on a 15-rung ladder and is judged twice — once on measured cost and counted structure, once on how good the frame looks at the rung its tier can afford.
perfContract:
THE CONTRACT. Binding on every piece. A piece that violates it is failed by a command, not by an opinion.

=== 1. THE FRAME WALL ===
Frame period: 16.667 ms, pinned AND capped.
- PINNED: total main-thread work <= 13.00 ms. The remaining 3.67 ms is inviolable slack for browser compositing, style/layout, GC and OS scheduling. Budgeting 16.67 of 16.67 is how you ship a stutter.
- CAPPED: the loop presents at most 60 times per second. On a 90/120/144 Hz display it renders every 2nd/3rd vsync. Free-running at 144 Hz is a FAIL, not a bonus. Measured as p01 frame interval >= 16.00 ms.

=== 2. CPU SUB-BUDGETS (ms, p95, measured at the tier's own emulated CPU rate) ===
  input + gesture resolution      0.20
  fixed-step sim (incl. windows)  2.60
  animation / pose / skinning     3.20
  FX + particle update            1.20
  camera + culling + LOD select   0.60
  render dispatch (JS side)       2.40
  overlay Canvas2D                1.80
  audio + misc                    0.30
  adaptive scaler + telemetry     0.10
  unallocated reserve             0.60
  ------------------------------------
  TOTAL                          13.00

These are absolute ms measured ON the tier's emulated CPU. On a 4x-throttled low tier the same wall applies, so the low tier must do roughly a quarter of the work. That is the honest translation of "pin at 60 on a slow phone," and this box can measure it for real: Chromium `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate` was verified here at rate=4 producing a measured 4.62x slowdown on a fixed workload.

=== 3. PACING TARGETS — identical on every tier, over a 60 s run, warmup excluded ===
  p50 frame interval        16.7 ms +/- 0.5
  p95                       <= 17.5 ms
  p99                       <= 20.0 ms
  worst single frame        <= 33.4 ms  (at most ONE dropped vsync, ever)
  dropped frames (>20 ms)   <= 0.5% of frames
  zero dropped frames in any 3 s window after the first 2 s
  PerformanceObserver longtask entries > 20 ms after warmup: ZERO
  p01                       >= 16.00 ms  (the 60 Hz cap)
Pacing is judged on the DISTRIBUTION. A mean of 16.7 with a hitch every 2 s is a failed game and this contract fails it.

=== 4. MEMORY / GC ===
  JS heap sawtooth amplitude over 60 s   <= 8 MB
  steady-state heap growth               <= 0.5 MB per 1000 frames
  per-frame allocation in the loop       ZERO (pools only; no closures, no array literals, no object literals, no string concat inside the frame path)
  texture bytes resident                 per-tier cap, section 6

=== 5. LATENCY (the timing axis) ===
  touch event timeStamp -> first frame whose sim state reflects it:
     p50 <= 2 frames (33.3 ms), worst <= 3 frames (50.0 ms)
  Input is sampled at the TOP of the frame, before the sim step, from a timestamped
  queue, and each event is assigned to the sim tick its own timestamp falls in — so a
  touch landing before the frame's step affects THAT step. Latency measured here is
  input -> render dispatch. The compositor-to-photon leg is NOT measurable on this box;
  assume +1 frame on a real device (see section 8, ASSUMPTION C).

=== 6. STRUCTURAL CAPS (the GPU axis — COUNTED, never eyeballed) ===
                          floor    low      mid      high
  draw calls (incl shadow)   60     110      180      280
  triangles                  90k    180k     400k     950k
  shader programs            12      18       26       38
  texture bytes resident     24 MB   48 MB    96 MB    192 MB
  render targets              1       2        3        5
  internal render scale     0.50    0.65     0.85     1.00
  DPR cap                   1.0     1.5      2.0      2.0
  shadow map                 off    512      1024     2048
  shadow caster draws          0     14       20       30
  post passes                  0      1        3        5
  live particles               0    400     1500     4000
  est. avg overdraw          1.6    2.0      2.6      3.4
  skinned actors (of 14)       6      10       14       14
  imposter actors              8       4        0        0
  quality rung range         0-2     3-6     7-11    12-15
Every scene object carries `userData.piece`, so `scripts/budget.mjs` attributes every
draw call and triangle to a piece by name. A piece that quietly adds 400 draw calls
FAILS a command and is named in the failure line.

=== 7. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A PIECE BLOWS IT ===
- CPU over p95 budget -> `perf.mjs` prints FAIL(<subsystem> p95) and exits 1. The piece
  is returned to its builder with the measured number and its budget line.
- Structural cap exceeded -> `budget.mjs` exits 1 naming the piece, the metric, the count
  and the cap. No screenshot is even taken; fidelity is not evaluated for an over-budget piece.
- Pacing tail failure (p99/worst/longtask) -> `perf.mjs` prints the offending frame index,
  its subsystem span breakdown and the longtask stack marker. Tail failures outrank mean failures.
- Latency failure -> `touch.mjs` exits 1 with per-gesture p50/worst in ms AND frames.
- Determinism failure -> `simtest.mjs` exits 1 with the first diverging tick.
- A piece may spend another piece's unused budget ONLY via the unallocated 0.60 ms reserve,
  and only with the reserve recorded in its own budget line. Silent borrowing is a FAIL.

=== 8. WHAT THIS BOX PROVES, BOUNDS, AND CANNOT PROVE ===
AXIS 1 — CPU: PROVEN HERE. Real 4-core CPU, real V8, real GC, real event loop.
  `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate` verified working (4.62x measured at rate=4). Every
  subsystem ms number, the heap sawtooth, the allocation-free assertion and the longtask
  tail are honest measurements that transfer to a phone's CPU.
AXIS 2 — FRAME PACING: PROVEN HERE, in `--raster=min` mode. Headless Chromium's rAF is
  vsync-locked at 60 Hz (verified: idle p50 = 16.70 ms), and an injected 90 ms hitch
  correctly produced max=83.30 ms, dropped=2, and one 90 ms longtask entry. That is the
  instrument working. It must run at a tiny internal render size (256x144, shadows off,
  post off) so that software raster is not the variable; what is then being measured is
  exactly the loop's tail behaviour, which is what transfers.
AXIS 3 — GPU: NOT PROVABLE HERE, AT ALL. Measured on this box: a shadowed
  MeshStandardMaterial scene costs roughly 100 ms per megapixel under SwiftShader
  (960x540 + 1024 shadow map = 83.3 ms; 780x1688 = 149.9 ms; 390x844 = 50.0 ms). To hit
  16.67 ms here we would need about 0.11 MP with shadows off — roughly 400x280. THIS BOX
  CANNOT RENDER THIS GAME AT 60 FPS AT ANY PLAYABLE RESOLUTION AND NO NUMBER MEASURED
  HERE IS A PHONE NUMBER. The GPU axis is governed ONLY by the counted structural caps in
  section 6, plus these declared assumptions:
  ASSUMPTION A — mid tier is an iPhone 12 / Pixel 6 / Snapdragon 778G class part. At
    0.85 render scale on a 2340x1080 panel (1.83 MP) with 2.6 avg overdraw that is
    4.75 Mpix/frame; assumed sustained ~2.0 Gpix/s effective for our shader complexity
    => ~2.8 ms GPU. ASSUMED. NOT MEASURED.
  ASSUMPTION B — mobile driver draw-call overhead ~0.012 ms each; 180 calls ~= 2.2 ms.
    The JS-side half of this IS measured here inside the 2.40 ms renderJS budget; the
    driver-side half is assumed.
  ASSUMPTION C — the compositor adds ~1 frame between our present and photons. All
    reported latency is input -> render dispatch; add one frame for a real panel.
  ASSUMPTION D — shader compile on a real mobile driver costs 5-50 ms per program and
    WILL stall a frame. Mitigation is measurable here and is a hard gate: all programs
    compiled and a dummy draw issued during the loading screen, and
    `renderer.info.programs.length` must not increase by even 1 after `flow.enterPlay()`.
AXIS 4 — THERMAL: PARTIALLY PROVABLE. Real sustained thermal throttling is not
  reproducible here, but its effect is: `perf.mjs --thermal-ramp` raises the CPU throttle
  rate 1x -> 4x mid-run and asserts the adaptive scaler steps down and pacing recovers
  within 1.0 s with <= 2 dropped frames. That is a real test of the real mechanism.

=== 9. THE TWO EXECUTION PATHS ===
  CAPTURE PATH (`?mode=capture`) — 1920x1080, ssaa 1.5, accum 32, half-float RT,
  preserveDrawingBuffer, ~20 s/frame. Judged ONLY on fidelity against the bar. NO frame
  budget applies. Unchanged, byte-deterministic, still the fidelity instrument.
  RUNTIME PATH (`?mode=play`) — direct to the default framebuffer, no accumulation RT,
  NO preserveDrawingBuffer, internal render scale from the quality tier. Judged ONLY on
  this contract. These are two paths against two bars and no result from one may ever be
  cited as evidence about the other.
deviceTiers:
FOUR TIERS, FIFTEEN RUNGS. Tiers are the coarse bucket used for structural caps and the harness's CPU-throttle emulation. Rungs are the continuous 0-15 quality ladder the runtime actually walks, so quality is smooth rather than four visible steps.

  floor  rungs 0-2    CPU throttle emulated at 6x    this container, llvmpipe/SwiftShader, old low-RAM Androids, any device that has thermally collapsed
  low    rungs 3-6    CPU throttle emulated at 4x    Mali-G52/G57, Adreno 610/619, iPhone 8/SE2 class
  mid    rungs 7-11   CPU throttle emulated at 2x    Adreno 64x/730, Mali-G78, A14/A15, Pixel 6 class
  high   rungs 12-15  CPU throttle emulated at 1x    A16+/M-series, Adreno 740+, desktop dGPU

=== HOW THE GAME DETECTS ITS TIER AT RUNTIME ===
Three stages. Stage 3 is the authority; stages 1 and 2 only pick a starting rung so the
first two seconds are not ugly or stuttering.

STAGE 1 — STATIC SIGNALS (< 2 ms, at boot, in `src/foundation/quality.js`)
  navigator.hardwareConcurrency (4 on this box)
  navigator.deviceMemory (UNDEFINED on iOS/Safari — verified undefined in this container's
    mobile-emulated context too; it must be treated as a bonus signal, never a requirement)
  devicePixelRatio, screen.width * screen.height, window.screen.orientation
  WEBGL_debug_renderer_info UNMASKED_RENDERER matched against a table:
    /SwiftShader|llvmpipe|Software/ -> floor (this box correctly self-identifies:
      "ANGLE (Google, Vulkan 1.3.0 (SwiftShader Device (Subzero)...)" )
    /Apple (A1[6-9]|A2|M[1-9])/ -> high;  /Apple A1[0-5]/ -> mid
    /Adreno.*(7[0-9]{2}|8[0-9]{2})/ -> high;  /Adreno.*6[2-9][0-9]/ -> mid;  else low
    /Mali-G(7[0-9]|[89][0-9])/ -> mid;  /Mali-G(3[0-9]|5[0-9])/ -> low
    unknown string -> mid, then let stage 2 correct it
  MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE, MAX_SAMPLES, EXT_color_buffer_float, EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2,
  and which of ASTC/ETC2/BPTC compression is present (a memory-ceiling proxy).

STAGE 2 — BOOT MICRO-PROBE (<= 250 ms wall, hidden behind the title screen)
  CPU probe: a fixed skinning-shaped workload — 14 actors x 26 bones x 200 iterations of
    quaternion slerp + matrix compose — timed with performance.now(). Yields ms/unit,
    which maps directly onto the animation budget line, because it is literally the work
    the animation subsystem does.
  GPU probe: render a known fill load (N full-screen quads with a fixed-cost fragment
    shader, N = 1,2,4,8) at the device's OWN resolution for 5 frames each, and take the
    slope of frame interval vs N. That yields an effective pixels/ms figure on the real
    hardware. This is the only honest way to learn what the GPU actually is, it needs no
    device database, and it works everywhere — on this box it will correctly report
    floor, which is the right answer here.
  Combined result -> starting rung.

STAGE 3 — CLOSED-LOOP ADAPTIVE SCALER (the authority; runs forever)
  Rolling 30-frame windows of measured frame interval and total CPU span.
  DOWN a rung: p95 interval > 17.5 ms for 2 consecutive windows (fast, because stutter is
    the thing we refuse to ship).
  UP a rung: p95 interval < 15.5 ms AND total CPU p95 < 9.0 ms for 8 consecutive windows
    (slow, hysteretic 8:2, so it never oscillates).
  Rate limit: at most one rung change per 3.0 s.
  A rung change is never applied mid-play in a way that can itself hitch: cheap rungs
  (particle count, render scale, shadow resolution) cross-fade over 250 ms; expensive
  rungs (post pass count, shadow on/off, actor LOD class) are queued and applied at the
  next play boundary, where a hitch is invisible.
  Never allocates, never compiles a shader (all programs for all rungs are pre-warmed at
  load — see ASSUMPTION D), never resizes a render target during a play.
  Thermal collapse is just a sustained DOWN sequence, and is tested by ramping the
  emulated CPU throttle mid-run.

=== WHAT SCALES BETWEEN TIERS, AND WHAT NEVER DOES ===
SCALES (rung-controlled, each piece implements `applyRung(n)`):
  internal render scale 0.50 -> 1.00; DPR cap 1.0 -> 2.0
  shadows: none (blob decals) -> 512 single cascade -> 1024 -> 2048
  volumetric shafts: off -> baked gradient haze -> camera-facing billboard shafts ->
    24-step raymarched with depth occlusion
  post: none -> grade only -> bloom+grade+vignette -> +DOF +motion blur +grain
  particles: 0 (a single sprite flash on impact) -> 400 -> 1500 -> 4000
  turf: flat-lit tiled -> tiled + normal map -> anisotropic + wet spec -> shell grass near camera
  crowd: baked backdrop texture -> scrolling imposter strip -> instanced quads ->
    instanced meshes with per-instance colour/height/slouch
  actors: 6 skinned + 8 imposter -> 10+4 -> 14 skinned -> 14 skinned + cloth/secondary motion
  bones evaluated: 14 (reduced chain) -> 20 -> 26 -> 26 + procedural secondary
NEVER SCALES — this is the answer to "still handsome at low tier." These cost almost
nothing and carry most of the perceived quality:
  the colour grade and its LUT, the value structure (near-black midtones, blown highlights
  only at sources and rims), the key-light direction and rim placement, silhouette and
  proportion, camera staging and composition, ALL typography and lettering, the HUD and
  callout layout, team colour identity, and the sim itself — every tier plays exactly the
  same game with exactly the same timing windows.
A floor-tier frame is a well-composed, correctly graded, sharply lettered arcade football
frame with simpler lighting. It is never a stuttering one.

perfCoreSpec.summary: PerfCore is the single agent allowed to unfreeze and rewrite the foundation. It builds the spine every other piece hangs off, and it builds the instruments every critic reads. Seven deliverables. (1) FRAME PACING LOOP (`loop.js`): a rAF-driven loop with a hard 60 Hz present cap (render every Nth vsync on 90/120/144 Hz panels), a monotonic wall clock, and named `performance.now()` spans around every subsystem, recorded into a preallocated ring buffer with zero per-frame allocation. (2) FIXED-TIMESTEP SIM CLOCK (`clock.js`): TICK = 1/60 s exactly, an accumulator with a hard catch-up clamp of 3 steps (beyond which time is DROPPED, never spiralled), a tick counter that is the single source of truth for every timing window, deterministic `seekTo(t)` for the capture path, and `stepN(n)` for headless Node unit tests with no renderer and no browser — verified importable: `src/foundation/*.js` and `three` both import cleanly under plain node v22. This replaces `engine.js:372` `liveT += SIM_STEP * 2`, which is frame-rate-dependent simulation and is the single worst defect in the current foundation. (3) TOUCH INPUT LAYER (`touch.js`): Pointer Events with setPointerCapture, `getCoalescedEvents()` for sub-frame accuracy, a timestamped lock-free event queue drained at the TOP of the frame, per-pointer tracking with correct pointercancel/touchcancel/visibilitychange/orientationchange release, `touch-action:none`, no-zoom/no-rubber-band/no-pull-to-refresh, `env(safe-area-inset-*)` resolution, and an input replay log keyed by (tick, action) so any session replays byte-identically. Foundation owns the RAW timestamped bus and the frame-boundary snapshot only; the `touch-controller` piece owns zones, gestures and feel. Keyboard/gamepad survive as a DEBUG-ONLY alias layer — the game must be fully playable with thumbs and nothing else. (4) ADAPTIVE QUALITY SCALER (`quality.js`): static signals + boot micro-probe + the closed-loop 30-frame-window rung scaler with 8:2 hysteresis and a 3 s rate limit, plus the `applyRung(n)` contract every visual piece implements, plus program pre-warm at load so no rung change ever compiles a shader. (5) STRUCTURAL BUDGET COUNTER (`budget.js`): counts draw calls, triangles, programs, texture bytes resident, render targets, particles and estimated overdraw, attributes every one to a piece via `userData.piece`, and asserts the per-tier caps. (6) PERF TELEMETRY (`telemetry.js`): the ring buffer, percentile computation, longtask observer, heap sampling, and the `window.__BLITZ_PERF__` read API. (7) ENGINE SPLIT (`engine.js`): `captureFrame()` stays exactly as it is — 1920x1080, accum 32, half-float, preserveDrawingBuffer, byte-deterministic. `runtime()` is NEW and renders direct to the default framebuffer with NO accumulation target and NO preserveDrawingBuffer, at the internal render scale the tier dictates. This is the highest-impact single change in the whole pass: measured on this box, the half-float RT + resolve-quad round trip alone costs +17 ms at 0.52 MP, and the current live path measures 200-566 ms/frame with only fallback content in the scene. PerfCore also extends `registry.js` PIECE_IDS and `src/pieces/index.js` to the new 18-piece set, adds the `controller`/`timing`/`flow` slots with working fallbacks, and adds `applyRung` to every slot interface. Then the foundation re-freezes.

PerfCore may not hand off until every one of these has been RUN and its output pasted into the handoff note. Nothing here is a claim; each is a command with an output.

1. SYNTHETIC LOAD AT EVERY TIER. Build a load generator that populates a scene to EXACTLY each tier's structural cap (N draw calls, M triangles, K particles, 14 actors at the tier's LOD mix, the tier's post pass count) using foundation fallback content only. Then `node scripts/perf.mjs --scene=perf_synthetic --tier=floor|low|mid|high --dur=60 --raster=min` must PASS all of section 3's pacing targets and hold TOTAL CPU p95 <= 13.00 ms AT THAT TIER'S THROTTLE RATE. That is the load-bearing proof: it demonstrates the loop holds the wall at 6x throttling with a floor-tier workload, which is the closest honest analogue to a cheap phone that this box can produce.

2. THE 60 Hz CAP, PROVEN WITHOUT A 120 Hz DISPLAY. `simtest.mjs --suite=clock` feeds the pacing accumulator a synthetic 120 Hz vsync sequence and asserts it presents on exactly every second tick and that the sim advances exactly 60 ticks per simulated second. Separately, `perf.mjs` must report p01 >= 16.00 ms on this box's real 60 Hz rAF.

5. ZERO-ALLOCATION FRAME LOOP. 3000 frames against a null scene: JS heap growth <= 0.5 MB per 1000 frames, sawtooth <= 8 MB, ZERO longtasks > 20 ms. Report the raw JSHeapUsedSize series.

6. THE COUNTER IS HONEST. Deliberately plant an over-budget object (an extra 400-draw-call group tagged `userData.piece='perfcore-canary'`) and show `budget.mjs` exiting 1 with the exact line naming the piece, the metric, the count and the cap. 7. PROGRAM WARM-UP GATE. Show `renderer.info.programs.length` unchanged across `flow.enterPlay()`, across a full rung sweep 0->15, and across a menu->play->menu round trip. This is the mitigation for the one mobile stall this box cannot otherwise see (ASSUMPTION D).

THE CAPTURE PATH IS UNBROKEN. `node scripts/shoot.mjs --all` must still produce 11/11 PNGs, and shooting one scene twice must still yield byte-identical output (the existing md5 is d96547de45fa9fc684fbfe8a00ea06f1). `node scripts/lint-determinism.mjs` must still pass with 0 errors. pieces.name: Touch Controller, Gestures & Thumb Layout
pieces.brief: You own the most important component of this game. Build the on-screen controller a player uses with two thumbs on a phone or tablet in landscape, with no keyboard, no hover, and no mouse. Left zone: a FLOATING virtual stick whose origin is set wherever the thumb first lands inside the zone (never a fixed pucks-on-glass stick), with a 6 CSS px deadzone, a 48 px full-deflection radius, radial clamping, and a re-center that follows the thumb if it drags past the radius. Right zone: the action cluster - a large primary (juke/dive/hit-stick, contextual on offense vs defense), a secondary (spin/stiff-arm), and turbo. Turbo is a HOLD, and it must be holdable while the stick is being moved: multi-touch is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have. Gestures: tap, swipe (8 directions), hold, and double-tap, disambiguated within 120 ms or 40 px of travel, whichever comes first, with an 8 px touch slop before a tap becomes a swipe. Consume the foundation's timestamped event queue at the top of the frame and emit an action stamped with the SIM TICK its own timestamp falls in - never the tick it happened to be read on. Handle every hostile case: pointercancel, touchcancel, a thumb sliding off the screen edge, a third finger landing, the notification shade being pulled, visibilitychange, orientationchange, and a palm resting on the display. Nothing may ever stick. Respect env(safe-area-inset-*) so a notch or a home indicator never eats a control. Draw the controller yourself into the overlay, and co-design its layout with hud-overlay: the bar art puts the TURBO meter bottom-left, which is exactly where the left thumb lives, so the meter moves up and out of the thumb zone while keeping its bar-matching styling. Everything you draw must be cached and blitted, not re-pathed per frame.
pieces.judgeOn: MEASURED. `node scripts/touch.mjs --tier=mid --gesture=all --viewport=844x390` must print: per-gesture latency p50 <= 2 frames and worst <= 3 frames; classification accuracy >= 98% over 200 scripted gestures per class; 100/100 simultaneous stick+button both registered; 0 stuck touches across 50 pointercancel, 50 slide-off-edge and 10 visibilitychange injections; all control zones within thumb reach at both 844x390 and 1024x768; and a 60 s scripted play completed with ZERO key events. `node scripts/perf.mjs` must show the input span p95 <= 0.20 ms and the controller's overlay share p95 <= 0.35 ms. Secondary and only after those pass: a still of the controller over a gameplay frame, judged for whether it reads as a real arcade controller rather than debug circles.

Overlay draw p95 <= 0.35 ms of the 1.80 ms overlay budget (cached layer blit; the stick ring, button glyphs and pressed states are pre-rendered once per rung to an offscreen canvas). 0 GL draw calls, 0 triangles, 0 shader programs, 0 texture bytes on the GL side; <= 1.0 MB of 2D canvas backing store. Zero per-frame allocation: attributable heap growth <= 0.05 MB per 1000 frames. Identical budget on all four tiers - the controller never degrades, because the controller is the game.

pieces.name: Action Timing Model (Tick-Exact)
pieces.brief: You own the thing the user called critical. Define every action timing window in the game in SIM TICKS at 1/60 s, never in milliseconds and never in frames, so that the model is exact, deterministic, replayable and testable with no renderer and no browser. Author the window table and the evaluator: juke (12-tick window opening when a defender is inside 2.2 m and closing, with a 4-tick perfect sub-window that grants a bonus and a longer i-frame), spin (14 ticks), stiff-arm (10 ticks, requires the defender inside arm reach on the correct side), dive (a 0-30 tick charge mapping to distance and to the risk of a fumble on contact), hit-stick (8 ticks before contact, with a punish window after), catch (16 ticks around ball arrival with a 5-tick perfect sub-window that upgrades a contested catch), pass lead (hold duration in ticks mapping to lead distance and arc), and turbo (burn per tick, recharge per tick, an overheat threshold, and a cooldown). Each window has an explicit open tick, close tick, perfect sub-range, the state predicate that arms it, the outcome tiers it produces, and the cancel rules that let one action interrupt another. Publish the whole table as data so the harness reads it rather than hard-coding it. Then make the feel legible: every window emits an event the HUD, FX and callout pieces consume so the player can SEE that they hit or missed - a timing game that does not tell you why you failed is a broken timing game. Guarantee that identical input at an identical tick from an identical seed produces an identical outcome, forever, and that a window's behaviour does not depend on the render frame rate in any way.
pieces.judgeOn: MEASURED, and this one runs in Node in about two seconds with no browser. `node scripts/simtest.mjs --suite=windows` must assert, for EVERY window, the exact open tick, close tick and perfect sub-range, with boundary tests at open-1 / open / close / close+1 all correct. The user's own example must appear verbatim as a passing assertion: input at t=1.000s (tick 60) LANDS and input at t=1.084s (tick 65) is classified exactly as the table says, with the first miss tick named. `--suite=determinism`: 10,000 seeded input replays must produce 10,000 identical state hashes. Frame-rate independence: the same replay stepped at a simulated 30, 60 and 144 Hz present rate must produce byte-identical outcomes. `perf.mjs` must show the window evaluator inside the sim span at <= 0.30 ms p95.
pieces.budget: <= 0.30 ms p95 of the 2.60 ms sim span, at every tier's throttle. 0 GL cost of any kind. Zero allocation - the window table is frozen at load and the evaluator writes into preallocated state. Identical on all four tiers: timing NEVER scales with device class, because two players on different phones must be playing the same game.

pieces.name: Fixed-Timestep 7-on-7 Arcade Simulation
pieces.brief: Make it an actual game, and make it advance in exact 1/60 s ticks driven by the foundation clock - never by the render frame. Implement deterministic 7-on-7 arcade football: offensive and defensive formations and alignment, the snap, route running with real route shapes (slant, go, post, corner, hook, wheel, drag), QB dropback and a throw with ball flight physics, catch and contest resolution, ball-carrier running with turbo, jukes, spins and stiff-arms driven entirely by the timing-windows table, defensive pursuit AI with real pursuit angles and man/zone assignments, gang tackling with a hit-power roll, fumbles, interceptions, downs, the first-down chain, the play clock and scoring including the arcade bonuses (TRUCK 150, WHAT A CATCH 175, LEVELER 200, TOUCHDOWN 200, MID-AIR MURDER 250). The entire simulation must run with ZERO allocation in the step function: all 14 actors, the ball, every route sample, every AI evaluation and every event record live in preallocated pools and typed arrays. Spatial queries use a fixed grid, not an O(n^2) sweep. All randomness comes from the seeded RNG stepped by tick, so a seed plus an input log fully determines the game. Expose `snapshot()` unchanged so the still-capture path keeps working exactly as it does today, and expose the per-tick event stream that FX, HUD, callouts and the camera consume. Design the AI so its cost is bounded and predictable rather than data-dependent: a fixed number of evaluations per tick, no early-out that turns into a spike when the play gets crowded. Worst-case tick cost matters more than average tick cost, because the worst case is what shows up in p99.
pieces.judgeOn: MEASURED FIRST, looked at second. `perf.mjs --tier=low` (4x throttle): sim span p50 <= 1.8 ms, p95 <= 2.30 ms, WORST <= 3.6 ms - the worst-tick number is the one that counts, because a data-dependent AI spike is a dropped frame. `simtest.mjs --suite=determinism`: 10,000 replays, identical hashes; and a 4-minute game replayed from seed + input log reproduces the final score exactly. Zero allocation: attributable heap growth <= 0.15 MB per 1000 frames. Only after all of that: shoot `live_play` at t=0.0/1.2/2.6/4.0 with a fixed seed and judge that the formation is legal at t=0, routes are distinguishable at t=1.2, pursuit angles are real at t=2.6, and there is a genuine tackle with FX at t=4.0.
pieces.budget: sim span (including timing-windows' 0.30 ms) p95 <= 2.60 ms, worst <= 3.6 ms, at every tier's throttle - so at 4x throttle the low tier must do a quarter of the absolute work of the high tier and the AI budget scales via evaluation count, never via tick rate. Sim tick rate is 60 Hz on ALL tiers, always. Catch-up clamped at 3 steps. 0 GL draw calls of its own. Heap: <= 6 MB of pooled state, allocated once at load.

pieces.name: Animation Runtime, Pose Library & Skinning LOD
pieces.brief: You own how bodies move AND what that movement costs. Two halves, and the second half is now the harder one. (1) The pose library: full 26-bone poses evaluated as a function of phase 0..1, plus procedural layers - breathing, spine lag, hand shaping, head look-at, foot planting - staged to match the bar panels: qb_dropback_throw, midair_tackle (fully horizontal, arms wrapping, victim's head snapping back), truck_carry (upright, driving, stiff-arm extended into a facemask), dive_catch_td (full-extension layout, arched back), leveler_hit, turbo_sprint, juke_left/right, spin, and the idle and locomotion set. (2) The runtime: evaluate and skin 14 actors inside 3.20 ms, which is the largest single subsystem budget in the game and the one most likely to blow. Build a bone LOD chain - 26 bones for actors inside the focal set, 20 for mid-distance, 14 for the reduced chain, and a static imposter pose for floor-tier background actors. Cache and reuse quaternion and matrix scratch; never allocate a Vector3 or Quaternion inside the frame. Write skinning matrices into a preallocated Float32Array and upload once per actor, not per bone. Animation must be a pure function of the SIM TICK, so it is identical whether the renderer presented that frame or dropped it, and so the still-capture path at ?t= keeps producing byte-identical frames. Implement applyRung(n) to select the bone LOD mix and whether secondary motion runs at all.

Zero allocation: attributable heap growth <= 0.10 MB per 1000 frames. Frame-rate independence: the same tick sequence produces identical bone matrices whether presented at 30, 60 or 144 Hz. THEN fidelity: `iso_poses` renders a 6-up contact sheet in flat grey - does truck_carry show a real driving stiff-arm with the defender displaced, is midair_tackle genuinely horizontal and airborne, is dive_catch_td a full-extension layout - scored against the matching bar panel, and `iso_pose_silhouettes` scored on silhouette alone.

pieces.name: Game Flow, Transitions & Hitch-Free Loading
pieces.brief: You own the fact that this is a playable game rather than a set of scenes, and you own the single mobile problem this container cannot otherwise see: the transition hitch. Build the state machine - boot, loading, title, team select, uniform, coin toss, playcall, pre-snap, live play, play result, score callout, halftime, game over - with the touch-driven navigation between them, a working back stack, and pause/resume on visibilitychange that clears every held touch and never spirals the sim clock on return. Own the loading screen and what happens behind it: bake every procedural texture, build every geometry, compile EVERY shader program for EVERY rung and issue a dummy draw for each, and run the quality boot probe, all before the title appears. After `enterPlay()` nothing may compile, nothing may allocate a render target, and nothing may bake a texture - those are the three things that stall a real mobile driver for tens of milliseconds and they are exactly what this box cannot measure, so they are forbidden structurally instead. Own the transition budget: entering a play from the playcall screen must not cost a single dropped frame, so pre-warm the play's actors, poses and FX pools during the playcall screen's idle time in bounded slices of at most 2 ms per frame. Own the play clock and the between-play cadence so the game has rhythm. Own the deterministic replay harness hook: seed plus input log reproduces a whole game.

pieces.name: Live HUD, TURBO Meter & Thumb-Safe Layout
pieces.brief: Draw the two persistent overlay elements from the bar, and draw them in under 1.10 ms every single frame. The top-left cluster: a dark angled beveled bar with slight transparency, containing a small stacked quarter/down block on a darker sub-panel, the game clock in white condensed numerals, two team chips each with a crest, a three-letter abbreviation and a large score numeral, and beneath each team name a thin momentum bar in that team's colour. The bottom-left TURBO meter: an angled plate with a beveled edge, TURBO in the techno face, and a segmented blue fill bar. The performance problem is that only a fraction of this changes per frame. Split the HUD into a STATIC layer (the plate, bevels, crests, team abbreviations, the TURBO chrome) baked once per rung into an offscreen canvas and blitted, and a DYNAMIC layer (clock digits, score numerals, momentum fill, turbo fill) redrawn into small dirty rectangles only when their value actually changes. Numerals come from typeface-lettering's rasterized glyph atlas as blits, never as path fills. The layout problem is that the bar puts TURBO bottom-left, which is precisely where the left thumb rests: co-design with touch-controller so the meter sits above the thumb zone, is never occluded by a hand, and still reads as the bar's plate. Resolve safe-area insets and support 16:9 through 21:9 without the cluster falling off the edge or into a notch. Add the timing feedback surface the timing-windows piece emits into: a perfect-window flash, a missed-window tick, and a turbo overheat state - the player must be able to see why a window was missed.

pieces.name: Runtime Camera, Post Ladder & Hero Staging
pieces.brief: Two halves, and the priority between them has inverted. (1) THE RUNTIME CAMERA is now the important half, because the camera is a timing and feel component: a sideline follow rig with velocity lead, dynamic FOV under turbo, impact shake with critically-damped decay, and a snap-zoom on big hits - all of it a pure function of the sim tick and all of it smoothed so it never introduces jitter of its own. A camera that judders at 60 fps reads as a dropped frame even when no frame was dropped, so the camera's own contribution to perceived pacing is part of what you are judged on. Own frustum culling and LOD selection: which actors are focal (26 bones, full material), which are mid (20 bones), which are reduced (14 bones), and which are imposters, recomputed on a bounded schedule rather than every frame for every object. (2) THE POST CHAIN becomes a rung ladder rather than a fixed stack: rung 0-2 no post at all; rung 3-6 a single combined grade pass; rung 7-11 bloom + grade + vignette in 3 passes; rung 12-15 adds bokeh DOF and motion blur for 5 passes. The grade itself - crushed teal shadows, warm blown highlights, high contrast, vignette - is applied at EVERY rung including rung 0, because the grade is nearly free and it carries most of the perceived quality; what scales is bloom quality, DOF and blur, not the colour script. Keep the ten hero ShotSpecs and the capture-path post exactly as they are: that path has no frame budget and should stay maximal. Implement applyRung(n) and never allocate or resize a render target after load.

pieces.name: Player Geometry, LOD Chain & Imposters
pieces.brief: Build the player body - geometry only, no materials, no posing - as a SkinnedMesh bound to the foundation's frozen 26-bone skeleton, procedurally generated per archetype (qb, skill, lineman, lb) with seeded variation in height, mass, limb length and musculature. The bar's players are exaggerated arcade-heroic: enormous shoulder pad flare, tapered V-torso, thick thighs, small waist, big hands. Model the gear as real geometry because it defines the silhouette - helmet shell with the correct dome and jaw profile, a tubular multi-bar facemask, chin strap, visor plane, shoulder pad shells with epaulettes and a clavicle gap, back plate, rib pads, forearm pads, thigh and knee pads, gloves, socks and cleats. Now the part that is new: you own a four-step LOD chain and its triangle budget. LOD0 focal (full detail, tubular facemask, separate glove and cleat geometry), LOD1 mid (merged gear, simplified facemask), LOD2 reduced (single merged mesh, card facemask), LOD3 imposter (a camera-facing textured quad baked at load from eight yaw angles, used for floor-tier background actors and for anyone beyond the LOD cut distance). All four must share the same silhouette read, because a popping silhouette is worse than a low-detail one - build the LOD transitions to cross-fade over 4 ticks. Merge geometry aggressively so 14 actors cost tens of draw calls rather than hundreds: one merged skinned mesh per actor at LOD0/1, one instanced batch for all LOD2 actors, one instanced batch for all imposters.

pieces.brief: Build the play-call screen, and build it as an in-game, time-critical, touch-driven screen rather than a poster. pieces.name: Turf Shader, Field Paint & Damage
pieces.brief: Own the ground plane, which is the single largest thing on screen and therefore the single largest fill-rate risk on a phone. Build a turf material that survives a low raking camera: mow-stripe banding, a wet specular sheen (the bar's field is glossy and reflects the light banks), and darkened saturated colour under moisture. Layer on field paint driven by a baked paint texture - yard lines every 5 yards, hash marks, numerals with directional arrows, sideline and end-line borders, a painted end zone in team colours with a fictional wordmark, and a midfield crest. Then damage: a dynamic decal texture accumulating divots with dark torn soil and scattered blades, cleat marks and skid streaks via addDivot/addCleatMark/addSkid, written into a small dirty region of an offscreen canvas rather than a full re-bake, because a full re-bake during a play is a dropped frame. Implement applyRung(n) as a real ladder: rung 0-2 a single flat-lit tiled draw with paint baked into the albedo and no damage at all; rung 3-6 tiled plus a normal map and damage decals; rung 7-11 anisotropic specular with the wet sheen and a stripe-aware normal; rung 12-15 adds shell-based grass geometry in a near-camera band only, with the shell count fading to zero by mid-field. pieces.name: Night Lighting, Volumetrics & Shadow Ladder
pieces.brief: Own every photon, and own the fact that lighting is where a mobile frame budget is usually lost. Build the night rig: banks of hot practical lights on the roof truss with flare-cored sources, a key that rakes players from behind-left to produce the hard white rim on shoulder pads and helmets seen in every action panel, a cool blue-violet sky fill, and warm bounce from the field. Then the atmosphere: volumetric shafts descending through haze, which is the most distinctive feature of the bar art and also the most expensive thing you could possibly do on a phone. So it becomes the sharpest rung ladder in the game: rung 0-2 no volumetrics and no shadow map at all - the shafts are baked into the sky/backdrop gradient and players get soft blob shadow decals; rung 3-6 a 512 single-cascade shadow on the focal actors only plus camera-facing billboard shafts with a soft depth fade; rung 7-11 a 1024 map, 20 caster draws, and billboard shafts with depth-aware occlusion so players carve into them; rung 12-15 a 2048 map, 30 casters, and 24-step raymarched shafts with real occlusion. The invariant across all four: the KEY DIRECTION, the rim placement and the value structure - near-black midtones with blown highlights only at sources and rims - are identical at every rung, because that is what makes the frame read as the bar, and it costs nothing. A rung-0 frame should look like a well-lit night game with simple shadows, not like a flat-lit one.

Is the value structure right? And `iso_light_rungs` at 0/4/9/15, where the rung-0 frame must still carry the same key direction, the same rim, and the same near-black midtones.

pieces.brief: Build the stadium that surrounds the field: a lower bowl, mezzanine and upper deck of raked seating wrapping 360 degrees, tunnel mouths, sideline benches, camera scaffolds, goalposts, pylons, sideline photographers, and a roof truss with light banks. pieces.name: Display Typefaces + Rasterized Glyph Atlas
pieces.brief: Your round-1 build stands: four vector display faces authored from scratch as glyph outlines, since no font on this box resembles the bar's type and no CDN is allowed. blitz-brush is the hand-lettered bold italic display face used for MID-AIR MURDER!, TRUCK!, TOUCHDOWN!, WHAT A CATCH!, CHOOSE YOUR CITY and DEFENSE! PICK A PLAY - a heavy right-leaning brush script with chiselled flat terminals, varying stroke weight, slightly irregular baselines, tapered exits and a rough torn edge, not a clean geometric italic. blitz-block is the condensed squarish HUD/label sans, blitz-num the tall gold numerals, blitz-techno the TURBO and tech labels. At load, and once per rung, rasterize every glyph of every face at the sizes the game actually uses into a packed offscreen atlas with its metrics table, and make faces.draw() a sequence of drawImage blits with kerning applied from the table. Keep the vector path API intact and unchanged for the capture path, which has no frame budget and should keep using outlines at full precision for maximum fidelity. So one piece, two rendering strategies, selected by execution path - exactly the split the whole plan now runs on. Include a fallback for a string the atlas does not cover so nothing is ever blank.

Pixel-identity: a string rendered via the atlas at its intended size must match the vector rendering within a stated per-pixel tolerance, so switching strategies does not change the art. pieces.name: Score Callout Lockups (Cached Blit Animation)
pieces.brief: Own the big hand-lettered score callouts - the loudest branding element in five of ten bar panels. Compose the lockup: line 1 in white with a heavy dark drop shadow and a thin dark outline; line 2 directly below in a punch colour (blood red for MURDER!, white for CATCH!/TOUCHDOWN!/TRUCK!/LEVELER! - study each panel); then a points line where the numeral is rich gold with a vertical gradient from bright gold to deep amber, a dark outline and a soft warm glow, followed by PTS in smaller white caps. Everything right-aligned in the lower right, rotated a couple of degrees, lines slightly overlapping, tracking tightened. The performance constraint changes how you build the animation. A callout is on screen for roughly two seconds during the most action-heavy, most FX-heavy, most likely-to-drop-a-frame moment in the game, and the drop shadows and glows you need are exactly the expensive Canvas2D operations. So compose each lockup ONCE into an offscreen canvas at the moment it is triggered - a single bake of at most 8 ms, which game-flow schedules into the play-result beat where a hitch is invisible - and then animate it per frame as a transform-only blit: translate, scale, rotate and alpha, with no re-compositing, no shadowBlur and no re-pathing. Author the entrance, hold and exit curves as functions of the sim tick so a callout is deterministic and reproducible. Add the timing-feedback variants the timing-windows piece emits, so a perfect-window catch reads visibly differently from an ordinary one.

Does the lettering carry a heavy drop shadow and rough brush edge so it punches off a busy background? iso_callout_over_bright tests exactly that against the brightest frame in the game.

pieces.name: Crests, Palettes, Wordmarks & Skylines
pieces.brief: Own the league's visual identity, which everything downstream consumes. Deliver eight fictional teams - NYC Strykers, CHI Maulers, DAL Outlaws, LA Titans, plus SEA, MIA, BAL and PHI - with full colour systems (primary, secondary, accent, helmet, metal) matched to the bar: Strykers teal/steel, Maulers red/black, Outlaws green/silver/white, Titans gold/black, plus purple, aqua and orange. The centrepiece is the crest generator: procedurally drawn vector emblems rendered to canvas at any size, matching the bar's team-select art - a stylized Statue of Liberty head in teal with a spiked crown; a snarling armored bulldog with a heavy jaw and visible teeth; a longhorn bull skull in white with dark curved horns; a gold-crested Spartan helmet - all with metallic bevel depth, an inner glow and a dark outline. Plus city skylines for backdrops, team wordmarks, and a fictional league mark (no real NFL shield, no real team marks). The budget constraint: crests are consumed by the HUD at chip size every single frame, by team select at card size, by the uniform sleeve as a texture, and by the end zone as paint. Rasterize each crest ONCE at load into a packed atlas at the three sizes actually used, publish the metrics, and make every consumer blit from the atlas. A crest that is re-pathed per frame in the HUD is a budget failure in someone else's piece caused by yours, so the atlas is the deliverable, not the path code.

retiredOrChanged:
Two pieces are RETIRED, two are NEW plus a third, one is MERGED away, and thirteen are RESCOPED. Net: 16 -> 18. Piece ids stay bound to the existing directory names wherever a piece survives, so the placeholder files and typeface-lettering's real round-1 build are preserved rather than thrown away. PerfCore extends `registry.js` PIECE_IDS and `src/pieces/index.js` to the new set during the unfreeze.

NEW (3) — these are the spine, and their absence is the plan's original defect:
- `touch-controller` (priority 1). Nothing in the original 16 owned input. `input.js` was 13 lines of keyboard KEYMAP plus a gamepad poll and it was frozen. The component the steer names most important had no owner, no brief, no budget and no critic.
- `timing-windows` (priority 2). Timing was implicit inside the sim brief as one clause among twenty. It is now its own piece with its own tick-exact table and its own Node-only, two-second, no-browser test suite — the cheapest and sharpest critic instrument in the whole set.
- `game-flow` (priority 5). Nobody owned the state machine, the loading screen, the pre-warm, or the transitions. That meant nobody owned shader-compile stalls, texture-upload spikes and transition hitches — the three mobile stalls this box cannot measure and must therefore forbid structurally.

RETIRED / MERGED (2):
- `menu-team-select` — retired, folded into `menu-title`, which now owns both front-end screens. Three separate menu pieces was an allocation made when fidelity was the top priority. Under the new ordering the front end is the least risky part of the project and does not deserve three parallel agents.
- The uniform SCREEN stays with `uniform-kit` rather than moving to a menu piece, because the screen exists to display the materials that piece authors; splitting them would have created a cross-piece dependency for no gain.

RESCOPED (13) — in every case the brief's visual content survives and a measured contract is added:
- `play-sim` — was judged on whether a formation looked legal in a screenshot. Now judged first on sim-span p95 AND worst-tick, zero allocation, and 10,000-replay determinism; the screenshot check is retained but demoted. Its AI must have bounded, data-independent cost, because a spike when the play gets crowded is a dropped frame.
- `pose-animation` — was a pose library. Now a pose library PLUS the animation runtime that owns the single largest CPU line in the game (3.20 ms), a four-step bone LOD chain and a zero-allocation skinning path.
- `hud-overlay` — was a pixel-match target. Now also owns thumb-safe layout (the bar puts TURBO exactly where the left thumb lives), a static-layer/dirty-rect split to fit 1.10 ms, and the timing-feedback surface that tells a player why they missed a window.
- `cinematography` — the two halves swapped priority. The runtime follow camera is promoted (it is a feel and timing component, and camera judder reads as a dropped frame even when none was dropped) and now owns culling and LOD selection. The post chain becomes a 0/1/3/5 pass ladder. The ten hero ShotSpecs and the unbudgeted capture-path post survive untouched.
- `impact-fx` — same visual brief, now a fixed-size pool sized once at load to the high-tier count, never grown, with additive overdraw counted because additive particles are the classic mobile fill-rate killer.
- `character-anatomy` — same silhouette brief, now owns a four-step LOD chain including baked eight-angle imposters, with a hard triangle and draw-call budget. It is the largest structural allocation in the game and the most likely quiet blowout.
- `turf-field` — same material brief, now with a rung ladder ending at a single flat-lit draw at floor tier, and damage decals restricted to dirty-region writes because a full re-bake during a play is a dropped frame.
- `stadium-lighting` — the volumetric shafts, the most distinctive feature of the bar art, are also the most expensive thing possible on a phone, so they become the sharpest rung ladder in the game: raymarched, billboard, baked gradient, off. The key direction, rim placement and value structure are invariant at every rung.
- `stadium-env` — collapses to a single baked backdrop draw at floor tier. It occupies the most pixels and is never in focus, so it must be the cheapest thing on screen.
- `uniform-kit` — same material brief, now with a hard cap of 6 shader programs at mid tier covering all eight teams times five variants. A per-variant program explosion is the specific failure mode and it is now counted, and the screen becomes touch-driven.
- `typeface-lettering` — the only piece with a real round-1 build, and it is KEPT intact. It gains a rasterized glyph atlas so runtime text is a blit, while the vector path API stays unchanged for the unbudgeted capture path. One piece, two rendering strategies, selected by execution path — the same split the whole plan now runs on.
- `score-callout` — same lockup brief, but the animation strategy is dictated by the budget: composed once into an offscreen canvas at trigger time, then animated as a transform-only blit with no shadowBlur and no re-pathing, because a callout is on screen during the most FX-heavy, most drop-prone two seconds in the game.
- `brand-identity` — same identity brief, but the deliverable becomes the rasterized atlas rather than the path code, because a crest re-pathed per frame in the HUD is a budget failure in someone else's piece caused by this one.

CROSS-CUTTING CHANGES TO EVERY SURVIVING PIECE:
1. Every piece implements `applyRung(n)` for the 0-15 ladder and is judged at its tier's rung, not at maximum.
2. Every scene object is tagged `userData.piece` so `budget.mjs` attributes every draw call and triangle by name.
3. Every piece carries numeric per-tier structural caps and, where it has runtime cost, a p95 and a WORST millisecond budget. The worst-case number is the binding one, because the tail is what a player feels.
4. No piece may create a shader program, allocate a render target, or bake a texture after `flow.enterPlay()`.
5. Fidelity is never evaluated for an over-budget piece: `budget.mjs` and `perf.mjs` gate the screenshot. A beautiful frame that costs 40 ms is not a partial success, it is a failure with a nice picture attached.
